title: Absolute and squared loss
goals: Explain how squaring changes sensitivity to large errors
Match the loss and units to the task

prerequisite.prompt: Which constant minimizes training squared error?
prerequisite.answer: The training mean among all constant predictions.

vocabulary: Square root of mean squared error
A numerical penalty for prediction errors

blocks.text: A loss summarizes error magnitude without positive and negative cancellation. MAE averages absolute residuals. MSE averages squared residuals and penalizes large magnitudes more strongly. RMSE takes the square root of MSE so it returns to the target unit. These are different questions, not interchangeable labels.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines absolute and squared loss.

Residuals [-1, 2,-3] cm have absolute errors [1, 2, 3], so MAE=6/3=2 cm. Squared errors [1, 4, 9] sum to 14, so MSE=14/3 square cm and RMSE=sqrt(14/3), about 2.16 cm. Keep the square and the average in the correct order.

blocks.title: Python 3 check
blocks.text:
from math import sqrt
residuals = [-1, 2, -3]
mae = sum(abs(r) for r in residuals) / len(residuals)
mse = sum(r * r for r in residuals) / len(residuals)
print(mae, mse, sqrt(mse))
# About 2.0, 4.67, 2.16.
# MAE and RMSE: cm. MSE: square cm.

Trace the calculation on paper before running this optional Python check. Use the stated fictional inputs and compare intermediate values. The code checks this example; your independent workbook case uses different evidence.

blocks.title: Absolute and squared loss at a glance
blocks.caption: Model A has residuals [0, 0, 6]; model B has [2, 2, 2]. Both MAEs are 2, but MSEs are 12 and 4. Squaring distinguishes concentrated large errors from evenly spread smaller errors. Which pattern matters depends on the task and consequences.

blocks.label: Give MSE and RMSE with units. Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: Changing cm to mm multiplies residuals and MAE/RMSE by 10, but MSE by 100. A loss decrease across reports is not meaningful unless units, evaluated rows and loss definitions match. Retain the per-record residuals for investigation.

Choose and document the comparison metric before reviewing final-test results. Neither MAE nor MSE reveals all subgroup patterns or proves safety. Do not remove a large valid error solely because it worsens squared loss.

workbook.prompt: Give MSE and RMSE with units.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: MSE 14/3 square cm; RMSE sqrt(14/3) about 2.16 cm.

workbook.title: Compare patterns
workbook.prompt: Why do [0, 0, 6] and [2, 2, 2] have equal MAE but unequal MSE?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Both absolute sums are 6. Squared sums are 36 and 12, so MSE 12 versus 4.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: Residuals [-2, 0, 4] m: calculate MAE MSE RMSE and the result of converting to cm.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: MAE 2 m; MSE 20/3 square m; RMSE about 2.58 m. In cm, MAE 200, MSE 200000/3, RMSE about 258.20.

workbook.title: Choose honestly
workbook.prompt: A team switches from MSE to MAE only after seeing a bad large error. What should be reported?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Keep the declared primary metric and disclose any additional metric and reason. Report the large error and complete evaluation.
